components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 消's meaning 'to disappear, dissolve,' like something dissolving in water.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound hint — 消 is pronounced xiāo, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
自 (nose) — the breath passing through.
心 (heart) — the breath of life, giving 息 its meaning 'to breathe; to rest; news.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ gāng shōudào yí gè hǎo xiāoxi.
example.english: I just received some good news.
example.fact: 消 alone means "to disappear, dissolve" and 息 means "to rest, breathe" — in classical Chinese 消息 first described the waxing and waning of the seasons or of yin and yang, an old astronomical sense that only later narrowed down to today's everyday meaning, "news."

components.note: 戈 (a spear or weapon) — 或 pictures defending a territory.
口 (here representing a walled area or territory) — defending one's territory with a weapon gave 或 its early sense of 'a certain place,' which later shifted to mean 'or,' offering an alternative.
讠 (speech) — 许 relates to giving permission through words.
午 (wǔ) gives a hint of the sound — 许 is pronounced xǔ, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他或许已经知道了这件事。
example.pinyin: Tā huòxǔ yǐjīng zhīdào le zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He may already know about this.
example.fact: 或许 sits at the more formal, written end of the "maybe" spectrum — 可能 and 也许 are the everyday spoken defaults, while 或许 shows up more in writing or careful speech, a register distinction the English gloss "perhaps" does not capture.

components.note: 女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'
匕 here relates to a person crouching or sitting — 此 originally pictured 'this place' where someone is.
止 (zhǐ) gives a hint of the sound — 此 is pronounced cǐ, sharing a similar final though the initial has shifted over time.

example.pinyin: Qíngkuàng bù yīnggāi rúcǐ zāogāo.
example.english: The situation shouldn't be this bad.
example.fact: 如此 is a formal, somewhat literary stand-in for the everyday 这么/那么 (both from the pilot batch) — it turns up constantly in writing and news broadcasts but sounds a little stiff in casual chat, where 这么 would be the natural choice.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.pinyin: Tā wúfǎ jiějué zhège wèntí.
example.english: He is unable to solve this problem.
example.fact: 无法 is always followed directly by a verb (无法解决 "unable to solve", 无法忘记 "unable to forget") and never by a bare noun — a learner reaching for 无法 the way English uses "no way to get a thing" will find the grammar does not work that way.

components.note: 户 (door) — 房 relates to a room or house, a space behind a door
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 房 is pronounced fáng, a close match
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Tāmen mǎi le yí tào xīn fángzi.
example.english: They bought a new house.
example.fact: 房子 takes the measure word 套 (a matched set) rather than the default 个 — 一套房子 is literally "one set of house," the same 套 used for a suit of clothes or a full set of dishes, treating a house as a complete bundle of rooms rather than a single countable item.

components.note: A drawing of a robe's collar and folded sides, seen from the front.
卩 (a person) — the one being dressed.
月 (a garment shape) — a hand 又 placing a coat on the person, giving 服 its meaning 'clothes; to obey, submit.'

example.hanzi: 这件衣服是我妈妈买的。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu shì wǒ māma mǎi de.
example.english: These clothes were bought by my mom.
example.fact: 衣 by itself is a pictograph of a robe's crossed collar and folded sides, and originally named an upper garment specifically — 衣服 broadened over time into a catch-all word for clothing in general, no matter which part of the body it covers.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — words spoken by a mouth are what reach the ear, giving 听 its meaning 'to listen.'
斤 stands in for the ear in this simplified character — the target that spoken words reach.
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.hanzi: 我听说他要搬到北京去了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ tīngshuō tā yào bān dào Běijīng qù le.
example.english: I heard he's moving to Beijing.
example.fact: 听说 reports something secondhand without vouching for it, and always opens the sentence (听说 + clause) — it never takes a direct object the way English "hear" can ("I heard the news" needs 听到 or 听见 instead, not 听说).

components.note: 彡 (shān) is the historical phonetic component of 参; sound change over time has left little resemblance to the modern reading cān
力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'

example.hanzi: 我们都参加了昨天的会议。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dōu cānjiā le zuótiān de huìyì.
example.english: We all attended the meeting yesterday.
example.fact: 参加 pairs with events you take part in (参加会议 "attend a meeting", 参加比赛 "enter a competition") — for joining an organization as an ongoing member, Chinese instead reaches for 加入, a common point of confusion since English "join" covers both.

components.note: 力 (strength) — relates to 办's meaning 'to handle, manage, do,' something accomplished through effort.
八 (bā) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from bàn.
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 我们得想个办法解决这个问题。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen děi xiǎng gè bànfǎ jiějué zhège wèntí.
example.english: We have to think of a way to solve this problem.
example.fact: 办法 almost always follows a "think of" verb — 想办法 ("think of a way") and 没办法 ("nothing can be done") are two of Mandarin's most common fixed phrases built on this word, the second doubling as a stock exclamation of resignation.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ wéiyī de péngyou.
example.english: She is my only friend.
example.fact: 唯 alone already means "only, alone" as a formal, literary word, and 一 means "one" — 唯一 doubles up "only" and "one" into a single emphatic word that sits directly before a noun, the way an adjective would.

components.note: 回 depicts a spiral or winding shape — something that turns back on itself, giving rise to the meaning 'to return.'

example.pinyin: Tiān hēi le, wǒmen gāi huíqu le.
example.english: It's getting dark, we should head back.
example.fact: 回去 pairs 回 ("to return") with the directional complement 去 ("away from the speaker") — swapping in 来 gives 回来 ("to come back, toward the speaker"), the same 来/去 vantage-point contrast that also splits 进来/进去 and 下来/下去 elsewhere in this batch.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.hanzi: 人们都喜欢在公园里散步。
example.pinyin: Rénmen dōu xǐhuan zài gōngyuán lǐ sànbù.
example.english: People like taking walks in the park.
example.fact: 人们 refers to people in general as a collective, almost always as the subject of a broad statement about society — it sounds odd for a small, specific group you can point to, where Chinese would just say 这些人 ("these people") instead.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 该's meaning 'ought to, should,' as if reached through spoken agreement.
亥 (hài) gives a sound hint — 该 is pronounced gāi, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant and tone differ.
匕 (a kneeling person) — a mourner bowed down in grief.
歹 (skeletal remains) — the corpse being mourned, the source of 死's meaning 'to die, dead.'

example.pinyin: “Gāisǐ! Wǒ bǎ yàoshi wàng zài jiā lǐ le.”
example.english: "Damn it! I left my keys at home."
example.fact: 该死 literally means "ought to die" (该 "should" + 死 "to die") — much like the English curse "damn it" (literally invoking damnation), its original violence has faded through overuse into a mild exclamation of frustration, not a real wish for anyone's death.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — 选 relates to the process of selecting, as if moving through options
先 (xiān) gives a sound close to 选's reading xuǎn

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yǒu hěn duō xuǎnzé.
example.english: We have many choices.
example.fact: 选择 works as both a verb ("to choose") and a noun ("a choice") with no change in form — 做选择 ("to make a choice") uses it as the object of 做, while 选择 placed before another noun or verb acts as the verb itself.

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 原 relates to a source high up, such as a spring emerging from rock.
泉 (quán) gives a hint of the sound — 原 is pronounced yuán, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 他没有说明迟到的原因。
example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu shuōmíng chídào de yuányīn.
example.english: He didn't explain the reason for being late.
example.fact: 原因 names the cause behind something and pairs naturally with 说明 ("to explain") or 找 ("to look for") — its counterpart 结果 ("result", also in this batch) often appears right alongside it in the fixed phrase 原因和结果, "cause and effect."

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí shuō xiàqù, méiyǒu tíng.
example.english: He kept talking on and on, without stopping.
example.fact: Beyond its literal "to go down" (走下去 "to walk down"), 下去 attached after almost any verb extends an action into the future — 说下去 ("keep talking"), 坚持下去 ("keep persisting") — an abstract extension mirroring what 起来 (pilot batch) does for actions just beginning, rather than continuing.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào hǎohǎo zhàogù zìjǐ.
example.english: You need to take good care of yourself.
example.fact: 好好 reduplicates the adjective 好 ("good") into an adverb meaning "properly, thoroughly" right before a verb — colloquially it's often extended with the diminutive suffix 儿 (好好儿) and a shifted spoken tone on the second syllable, a common spoken variant that written pinyin references don't always show.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.

example.pinyin: Tā quèshí hěn nǔlì.
example.english: He really is very hardworking.
example.fact: 确实 confirms that something is true or accurate, often responding to doubt — unlike 真的, its more casual spoken counterpart, 确实 leans formal and shows up more often in writing, news, and considered speech.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 混 originally described muddy, mixed water.
昆 (kūn) gives a sound distantly related to hùn, having drifted apart over time.
虫 (a small creature) — 蛋 names an egg, historically grouped together with small creatures like insects and reptiles.
延 (yán) is only distantly related in sound to dàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.pinyin: “Nǐ zhège húndàn!” tā shēngqì de shuō.
example.english: "You bastard!" she said angrily.
example.fact: 混 is read here with its colloquial second tone hún ("muddled, foolish") rather than its more common fourth-tone reading hùn ("to mix"). 蛋 ("egg") is one of Mandarin's most productive insult suffixes, also seen in 坏蛋 ("bad egg, scoundrel") and 笨蛋 ("fool," literally "stupid egg").

components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.
讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'

example.hanzi: 我向你保证,这件事不会再发生。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xiàng nǐ bǎozhèng, zhè jiàn shì bú huì zài fāshēng.
example.english: I guarantee you, this won't happen again.
example.fact: 保证 introduces a promise and is almost always followed directly by the content of that promise as a full clause — "我向你保证..." ("I guarantee/promise you that...") is a fixed, formal way to open a solemn assurance.

components.note: 冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.
木 (wood) — 校 originally related to a wooden framework, later coming to mean 'school,' a place of structured learning
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to 校's reading xiào

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǒulù qù xuéxiào.
example.english: I walk to school every day.
example.fact: 学 pictures children (子) gathered under a roof (冖) to study, and 校 originally meant a wooden framework or enclosure before narrowing to "a place of structured learning" — 学校 combines "studying" with "an enclosed place" into a fairly transparent image of the institution itself.

meanings: to accept (a suggestion, punishment, bribe etc)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.
爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'

example.pinyin: Tā hěn nán jiēshòu zhège shìshí.
example.english: He finds it hard to accept this fact.
example.fact: 接受 means to accept something once offered — an apology, a gift, an idea — while 接 alone just means "to receive" without any sense of agreement; adding 受 ("to bear, to undergo") is what pushes the word from mere receiving into willingly taking something on.

components.note: 己 (a kneeling child) — the one being disciplined.
攵 (a hand with a stick) — correcting the child, giving 改 its meaning 'to change, correct, reform.'

example.hanzi: 这件事改变了我的想法。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì gǎibiàn le wǒ de xiǎngfǎ.
example.english: This changed the way I think about it.
example.fact: 改变 describes a shift into a genuinely different state (改变想法 "change one's mind", 改变计划 "change plans") — for a smaller correction, like fixing a typo, Chinese instead reaches for the narrower root character 改 that 改变 itself is built from.

components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Kànlai tā jīntiān bú huì lái le.
example.english: It looks like he won't be coming today.
example.fact: 看来 almost always opens a sentence as a stand-alone adverb, signaling the speaker's own inference from visible evidence ("from how it looks...") — distinct from 好像 ("it seems, as if"), which can sit mid-sentence and does not necessarily imply the speaker reasoned it out from something observed.

components.note: 广 (shelter) pictures a drying shed.
林-shaped strokes below picture hemp fibers hung to dry, giving 麻 its meaning 'hemp.'
火 (fire) — 烦 describes a burning, irritated feeling.
页 (yè) gives a sound distantly related to fán, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Máfan nǐ bāng wǒ kāi yíxià mén.
example.english: Could you please help me open the door?
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense "trouble, hassle," 麻烦 doubles as one of Mandarin's most common polite openers for a request — 麻烦你... ("sorry to trouble you, but...") softens an imposition the same way English "sorry to bother you" does before asking a favor.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.hanzi: 天上突然出现了一道彩虹。
example.pinyin: Tiānshàng tūrán chūxiàn le yí dào cǎihóng.
example.english: A rainbow suddenly appeared in the sky.
example.fact: 出现 describes something coming into view or into existence for the first time (出现问题 "a problem arises") — its cousin 表现 (also in this batch) instead describes how something behaves once it is already there, a distinction easy to blur since both share the character 现.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
⺮ (bamboo) — the material of ancient counting rods.
具 (held in two hands) — bamboo counting rods or an abacus held up for use, the tools of calculation that gave 算 its meaning 'to calculate, count.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ shǔjià dǎsuàn zuò shénme?
example.english: What do you plan to do for summer vacation?
example.fact: 打算 signals a fairly loose, still-flexible intention ("what I'm thinking of doing"), a notch less firm than 计划 ("plan"), which implies something more deliberately mapped out — asking 你打算做什么 sounds more casual than asking 你有什么计划.

components.note: 电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
彡 (fine lines) — suggests light and shadow, relating to 影's meaning 'shadow, image.'
景 (jǐng) gives a sound hint — 影 is pronounced yǐng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhōumò qù kàn diànyǐng ba.
example.english: Let's go watch a movie this weekend.
example.fact: 电影 literally means "electric shadow" (电 "electricity" + 影 "shadow, image") — coined when film was a genuinely new technology, the same "electric ___" pattern that produced 电话 ("electric speech," telephone) and 电脑 ("electric brain," computer).

components.note: 身 depicts a person's torso, originally showing a pregnant woman's body — later broadened to mean 'the body' in general.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.pinyin: Nǐ shēnshang yǒu méiyǒu dài qián?
example.english: Do you have any money on you?
example.fact: 身上 literally means "on the body," but its most common everyday use asks whether someone is carrying something on their person right now (身上有钱吗 "do you have money on you") — functionally closer to English "on me/on you" than to any literal reference to skin or clothing.

components.note: 户 (door) — 房 relates to a room or house, a space behind a door
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 房 is pronounced fáng, a close match
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo yíxià.
example.english: Please clean up the room a bit.
example.fact: 房间 names a single enclosed room within a larger building (一个房间 "a room") — for the building or dwelling as a whole, Chinese instead uses 房子 (also in this batch), a whole/part distinction that English blurs by using "room" loosely for both in casual speech.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
⺮ (bamboo) — 管 originally referred to a bamboo pipe or tube, later broadening to mean 'to manage' or 'to control.'
官 (guān) gives a hint of the sound — 管 is pronounced guǎn, a connection that has shifted only slightly in tone.

example.hanzi: 不管天气怎么样,我们都会去。
example.pinyin: Bùguǎn tiānqì zěnmeyàng, wǒmen dōu huì qù.
example.english: No matter what the weather is like, we'll go.
example.fact: 不管 sets up a "no matter what" clause that is regularly completed later in the sentence by 都 ("in every case") — the same "no matter...都..." skeleton that 无论 also uses, making 不管 one half of a fixed two-part frame rather than a word that stands alone.

components.note: 牛 (ox) — 特 originally referred to a male ox singled out for sacrifice, a special animal set apart from the herd.
寺 (sì) gives a hint of the sound — 特 is pronounced tè, a connection that has drifted over time.
另 (other, separate) — 别 relates to distinguishing one thing from another.
刂 (knife) — cutting things apart to sort them gave 别 its meaning 'to separate' or 'other,' and later, 'don't' as a command.

example.pinyin: Zhège dìfang tèbié ānjìng.
example.english: This place is especially quiet.
example.fact: 特别 works two ways: as an adjective meaning "special, unusual" describing a noun (特别的礼物 "a special gift"), and as an intensifying adverb before another adjective meaning "especially" (特别安静 "especially quiet") — the same word doing two different jobs depending on where it sits.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 注 relates to pouring or directing, like water poured into something
主 (zhǔ) gives a sound close to 注's reading zhù
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.hanzi: 过马路的时候要注意安全。
example.pinyin: Guò mǎlù de shíhou yào zhùyì ānquán.
example.english: When crossing the road, pay attention to safety.
example.fact: 注 by itself means "to pour, to direct toward," as water is directed into a vessel, and 意 means "mind, intention" — 注意 pictures directing one's mind toward something, the same "directed attention" image behind the English idiom "pay attention."

components.note: 至 depicts an arrow reaching the ground after landing — arriving at a destination gave 至 its meaning 'to arrive' or 'until.'

example.hanzi: 他忙得甚至没有时间吃饭。
example.pinyin: Tā máng de shènzhì méiyǒu shíjiān chīfàn.
example.english: He's so busy he doesn't even have time to eat.
example.fact: 甚至 pushes a statement to its most extreme, surprising case ("even...") and often pairs with 都 or 也 later in the sentence for emphasis — it leans more formal than the everyday 连...都... construction, which does very similar work in casual speech.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.
扌 (hand) — represents the act of guarding or defending.
户 (door/household) — protecting one's home gave 护 its meaning 'to protect, guard.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi bǎohù huánjìng.
example.english: We should protect the environment.
example.fact: 保护 protects something from harm before it happens — the environment, one's eyes, a species — while 保证 (also in this batch, sharing the character 保) instead guarantees an outcome or promise; both build on 保's core sense of "to look after," just applied to physical safety versus a spoken assurance.

components.note: 直 (straight, upright) — 真 relates to something level and true.
几 (a small table) — an object placed level and true on a table gave 真 its meaning 'real' or 'true.'
一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'

example.pinyin: Tā cái shì zhēnzhèng de péngyou.
example.english: He is a true friend.
example.fact: 真 and 正 are near-synonyms on their own — 真 means "real, true" and 正 means "correct, upright" — 真正 reinforces the two into one emphatic word, the same doubling-up strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该 from the pilot batch, just with a different pair of near-synonyms.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 结 relates to tying or knotting threads together.
吉 (jí) gives a hint of the sound — 结 is pronounced jié, a connection that has shifted over time.
田 (here representing round fruit, not its usual meaning 'field') — 果 pictures fruit hanging from branches.
木 (tree) — fruit growing on a tree gave 果 its meaning 'fruit' and, more broadly, 'result.'

example.pinyin: Kǎoshì jiéguǒ míngtiān gōngbù.
example.english: The exam results will be announced tomorrow.
example.fact: 结果 has two distinct readings that CEDICT sources can blur: read jiéguǒ (结 in its common jié tone, "to tie, to form"), it means "result, outcome" and is one of the most frequent nouns in Mandarin — while read jiēguǒ (结 in the rarer jiē tone), it instead means literally "to bear fruit," describing a plant. The high-frequency word behind this entry is the jiéguǒ "outcome" sense, not the far rarer horticultural jiēguǒ.

components.note: 毛 (fur, hair) — 表 originally pictured a fur garment worn on the outside.
衣 (clothing) — an outer fur wrap gave 表 its meaning of 'outer' or 'surface,' and later, 'to express' (showing something on the surface).
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.hanzi: 他在比赛中表现得很好。
example.pinyin: Tā zài bǐsài zhōng biǎoxiàn de hěn hǎo.
example.english: He performed very well in the competition.
example.fact: 表现 works as a verb ("to perform, to behave") and a noun ("performance") without changing form — 表现得很好 uses it as a verb followed by a manner complement, while 他的表现很好 uses the exact same word as the subject noun of the sentence.

example.pinyin: Wǒ qíshí bú tài xǐhuan kāfēi.
example.english: Actually, I don't really like coffee.
example.fact: 其实 typically introduces a mild correction or a truth that contradicts what was just said or assumed ("actually, the truth is...") — a common way to soften disagreement or a surprising admission without directly contradicting the other person outright.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn, dìshang hěn huá!
example.english: Be careful, the floor is slippery!
example.fact: 小 means "small" and 心 means "heart, mind" — 小心 literally pictures keeping one's mind small and tightly focused on a task, rather than "small-hearted" in the English sense of stingy or cowardly; the compositional logic runs the opposite direction from what an English speaker might guess.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng jìnlái zuò yíhuìr.
example.english: Please come in and sit for a while.
example.fact: 进来 pairs 进 ("to enter") with 来 ("toward the speaker"), said by someone already inside inviting someone in. Swapping in 去 instead gives 进去 (also in this batch), reversing the viewpoint to "entering, away from the speaker" — the same 来/去 contrast found in 回来/回去 and 下来/下去.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.hanzi: 我当时并不知道发生了什么。
example.pinyin: Wǒ dāngshí bìng bù zhīdào fāshēng le shénme.
example.english: At the time, I really didn't know what had happened.
example.fact: 当时 always points back to a specific past moment already established in the conversation ("at that time, back then") — unlike 现在 ("now," from the pilot batch), which anchors to the moment of speaking, 当时 can never refer to the present.

meanings: (used to express lack of alternatives) can only

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the source of speech.
八 here suggests something small or simple leaving the mouth, giving 只 its meaning 'only, merely.'
月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.pinyin: Tā zhǐyǒu yí gè mèimei.
example.english: He only has one younger sister.
example.fact: 只有 frequently sets up a "the only way is..." clause completed later by 才 ("only then"), as in 只有努力才能成功 ("only through hard work can one succeed") — a fixed two-part frame parallel to 不管...都... elsewhere in this batch, where a first half sets a condition and a later adverb locks it in.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 怎's meaning 'how' relates to a mental inquiry, what's on one's mind.
乍 (zhà) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zěn.
力 (strength) — relates to 办's meaning 'to handle, manage, do,' something accomplished through effort.
八 (bā) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from bàn.

example.hanzi: 如果他不同意,我们怎么办?
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ tā bù tóngyì, wǒmen zěnmebàn?
example.english: If he doesn't agree, what should we do?
example.fact: Built from 怎么 ("how," pilot batch) plus 办 ("to handle"), 怎么办 literally asks "how to handle it" — but it is just as often blurted out completely alone, as a one-word cry of "What do I do?!", functioning as a stand-alone exclamation of panic as much as a real question.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绝 originally meant to sever a thread completely, extended to mean 'to cut off, absolute'
色 (sè) gives a loose sound connection to 绝's reading jué
又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.pinyin: Zhè juéduì shì gè hǎo zhǔyi.
example.english: This is absolutely a good idea.
example.fact: 绝 alone means "to cut off completely, to sever" — the same "cutting off" sense shows up in 拒绝 ("to refuse," literally "to sever/resist") — an image of severing all alternatives that gives 绝对 its sense of "no exceptions, no room for doubt."

meanings: sir (term of address for senior officer)

components.note: 长 (simplified from 長) depicts an elderly figure with long flowing hair and a cane — length and seniority are linked in the original picture.

example.pinyin: “Shì, zhǎngguān!” shìbīng dàshēng huídá.
example.english: "Yes, sir!" the soldier replied loudly.
example.fact: 长 is one of Mandarin's most common heteronyms: read zhǎng (as here) it means "chief, head, elder" (长官 "commanding officer," also 校长 "principal"); read cháng it instead means "long" in length or duration (长城 "the Great Wall") — one character splitting into two unrelated meanings depending on tone.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.

example.hanzi: 他敲了敲门,然后走了进去。
example.pinyin: Tā qiāo le qiāo mén, ránhòu zǒu le jìnqù.
example.english: He knocked on the door, then walked in.
example.fact: 进去 completes 进 ("to enter") with 去 ("away from the speaker") instead of 来 — said from the perspective of someone outside, or narrating someone else moving further inside, the mirror image of 进来 earlier in this batch.

components.note: 至 depicts an arrow reaching the ground after landing — arriving at a destination gave 至 its meaning 'to arrive' or 'until.'
少 depicts a few small dots or grains, like scattered sand — a simple picture of a small quantity, giving the meaning 'few' or 'little.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ zhìshǎo yīnggāi shuō shēng xièxie.
example.english: You should at least say thank you.
example.fact: 至 means "to arrive, to reach a limit" and 少 means "few, little" — 至少 literally pictures "reaching down to the smallest amount," the lower bound of what's acceptable, a logic mirrored by its opposite 至多 ("at most," reaching up to the largest amount).

components.note: 彳 (to walk/step) — represents movement or conduct.
聿 (an old form related to a writing brush) — conduct guided by written rules gave 律 its meaning 'law, regulation.'
帀 (a banner or covering) — flying above the scene.
刂 (a knife) — wielded with skill beneath the banner, an image of expertise giving 师 its meaning 'master, teacher, expert.'

example.hanzi: 她请了一位律师帮她打官司。
example.pinyin: Tā qǐng le yí wèi lǜshī bāng tā dǎ guānsi.
example.english: She hired a lawyer to help her with her lawsuit.
example.fact: 律师 takes the respectful measure word 位 rather than the neutral 个 (一位律师, not 一个律师) — the same polite 位 used for teachers and doctors, a small measure-word choice that signals respect for the profession.

components.note: 敕 (an order, discipline) — relates to 整's meaning 'orderly, whole, to arrange.'
正 (zhèng) gives a sound hint — 整 is pronounced zhěng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.pinyin: Tā zhěnggè xiàwǔ dōu zài shuìjiào.
example.english: He slept the whole afternoon.
example.fact: 整个 always sits directly before a noun as a modifier (整个下午 "the whole afternoon", 整个城市 "the whole city") and cannot stand alone as a full predicate the way 所有 (pilot batch) sometimes can — the two "whole/all" words divide the grammatical labor of English "whole" and "all" between them.
